newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX crude settles lower but downside limited.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX crude settles lower but downside limited.

text.p: NYMEX crude oil ended lower Friday after news Iraq would suspend military action sent prices lower late session, but selling was limited by a market perception that the U.S.-Iraq conflict was not over, traders said.
"It lead to light long liquidation, but clearly this situation is not over," said Thomas Blakeslee of Cargill Investor Services.
October crude ended off 49 cents to $24.51 a barrel.
Iraq said it would halt attacks on U.S. jets patrolling U.S. "no-fly zones" in northern and southern Iraq.
"That just set off profit-taking. It was whole the story," said a trader.
October heating oil closed down 1.23 cents to 67.94 cents a gallon, and October gasoline closed off 1.31 cents to 64.60 cents a gallon.

After Iraq said it would suspend military attacks, the White House said it would judge Iraq on its actions. The market had been anticipating possible missile strikes by the United States against Iraq after Iraq shot missiles at U.S. jets flying over a northern no-fly zone. The United States and its allies set that no-fly zone after the 1991 Gulf War.

Earlier in Friday's session, October heating oil set a life-of-contract high of 70.15 cents and October crude oil set a life-of-contract high of $25.35, but Iraq's statement sent prices into reversal.
"There was no follow through after we got to that level and it had run out of steam, so when the news came in, it pulled back," said a trader.
Dealers said Friday's options expiry for the October crude contract sent the price near the strike of $24.50.

The post-Gulf War high for crude is $25.70 and 72.25 cents for heating oil, though traders said oil prices were news driven at the moment, so they could not predict if and when those highs would be broken.

Heating oil has traded sharply higher on distillate stocks being at historically low levels, and at least one trader thought October heating oil could rise to 72.00 cents on fundamentals alone next week.

Iraqi conflict has delayed the oil-for-food deal further, dealers said, but some saw crude oil as overbought considering the conflict has not disrupted oil output in the Middle East region, the world's key supplier of oil.
However, traders said events in Iraq remain uncertain making heavy selling too risky.
Support for October crude was pegged near $24.25.
-- Harry Milling, New York Energy Desk, 212-859-1761
